lead.headline: In Manila, the Quad Backs Minerals Deals and a 2027 Patrol Exercise
lead.deck: Trump, Modi, Takaichi and Albanese met on 17 November and opposed changing the regional status quo by force or coercion.
body: The leaders of the Quad, a grouping of the United States, India, Japan and Australia, met in Manila on Tuesday 17 November, towards the end of the ASEAN summit. Donald Trump, Narendra Modi, Sanae Takaichi and Anthony Albanese attended; CNN called it the Quad’s first leader-level meeting since Trump took office, and it was Takaichi’s first. Modi noted that the Quad was founded in Manila nearly 20 years ago.

The headline outcome was on critical minerals, raw materials such as lithium, cobalt and nickel that batteries depend on but whose supply carries risks. Trump announced agreements he said would prevent “coercion by any single foreign supplier”, without naming the partners, the minerals or China, which dominates global rare earth supplies.

On security, the four countries’ P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft will fly in a maritime exercise in 2027, the first in a Quad setting, and a new Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration will share information. The joint statement opposed changing the status quo by force or coercion and voiced “grave concerns” about economic coercion, without naming any country.

On technology, the Quad is launching an AI accelerator and spending more than $85 million to widen access to trusted AI across the Indo-Pacific. The leaders also announced cybersecurity cooperation, welcomed an expansion of Australia’s role in the Quad’s cable partnership to cover electricity cables, and set the first Quad Business Leaders’ Forum for early 2027.
At the East Asia Summit the same day, Modi announced a Seafarers’ Safety Initiative for joint training and emergency response. Trump now moves on to Shenzhen for APEC.

world.headline: Ukraine Brings Down a Road Span of the Kerch Bridge, Two Days Before the Shenzhen Summit
world.deck: Kyiv says one steel arch and the road beneath it were destroyed; the Kremlin calls the damage minor and promises repairs.
body: Ukrainian drones and missiles struck the Kerch Bridge for a second night running, and on Tuesday 17 November brought down its main road arch. The bridge crosses the Kerch Strait to link Russia’s mainland with Crimea, which Russia seized from Ukraine in 2014. Putin opened it in 2018; it cost $3.7 billion and was built to carry 40,000 cars a day. The road bridge is about 16.9 km long, and a parallel railway bridge, opened to freight in 2020, about 18.1 km.

Ukraine’s SBU security service said one of the metal arches and the road span beneath it were destroyed. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian long-range drones struck the road section, while Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the railway, and Flamingo missiles delivered the final blow. He described the strike as the seventh stage of an operation lasting several weeks. Russia’s Transport Ministry said rail traffic had resumed on one track.

Moscow played the damage down. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said traffic continued and the bridge would be “even better than before”, and Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said a government commission had discussed delivering cargo to Crimea by alternative routes. Russia’s Investigative Committee called the strike a “terrorist act”; the Transport Ministry said there were no casualties. The air war also widened overnight: Russia said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones, and Zelenskyy said seven Russian ballistic missiles hit two of Kyiv’s main bridges.

How much the strike matters militarily is debated. The Institute for the Study of War said it was likely part of Kyiv’s campaign to deny Russian forces major supply routes via Crimea, but the bridge was once a key supply route and Russia’s military now relies more on a land corridor. The span also crosses a channel used by ships entering and leaving the Sea of Azov, so the collapse could substantially delay any return of shipping from that sea. The strike came two days before Putin was due to meet Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

india.headline: Cyclone Akvan Is Forecast to Hit the Andhra Coast as a Very Severe Storm Around Noon on 20 November
india.deck: The IMD expects winds of 120-130 km/h gusting to 145 km/h; Odisha has begun evacuations and fishing is suspended in the Bay of Bengal.
body: Cyclone Akvan, which formed when a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal intensified into a cyclonic storm, is expected to keep strengthening as it approaches India’s east coast. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects it to become a Severe Cyclonic Storm around the evening of 17 November and a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm around the morning of 19 November. The IMD’s 17 November bulletin placed it about 610 km east of Chennai and 660 km southeast of Machilipatnam.

Landfall, the moment a storm’s centre crosses the coast, is forecast around noon on 20 November, on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni, though the forecast may change. The IMD expects sustained winds of 120-130 km/h gusting to 145 km/h at that point, and has warned of extensive damage in coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh and of a possible storm surge, a rise in sea level pushed ashore by the storm, of 1-2 metres in low-lying parts of Prakasam, Bapatla, Krishna, West Godavari, Konaseema and Kakinada districts. Coastal Andhra Pradesh could see isolated extremely heavy rainfall of more than 21 cm on 19 and 20 November, and Odisha heavy rain at isolated places between 19 and 21 November.

Preparations are under way. An Orange Message has been issued for the Andhra Pradesh and adjoining south Odisha coasts. Odisha has started moving people out of vulnerable areas, ordering evacuations in six districts according to a Daily Jagran live tracker. The IMD has advised fishermen not to venture into the northwest, southwest and west-central Bay of Bengal until 20 November, and fishing is to be suspended completely in the warning zones.

State governments are preparing for impact. In Andhra Pradesh, which was recently hit by Cyclones Arnab and Murasu, Chief Minister Naidu and Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan reviewed preparedness. Pawan Kalyan told officials to set up relief camps stocked with food and drinking water, and to clear fallen trees and repair roads, while Naidu asked for rescue and rehabilitation to proceed based on real-time assessments.

The storm’s name was contributed by Iran. Names for North Indian Ocean cyclones come from a list shared by 13 countries under the WMO-ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones, and the IMD’s Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre in New Delhi assigns them. Akvan is the third storm in quick succession, after Arnab and Murasu; the next name on the list is Kaani.

politics_and_civics.headline: Schumer Says He Has the Votes to Stay Senate Democratic Leader Ahead of a 1 December Secret Ballot
politics_and_civics.deck: Challenger Chris Van Hollen claims 15 votes; because the ballot is secret, public endorsements show only part of the race.
body: In the US Senate, each party’s senators choose their own leader; voters do not. Democrats recaptured the Senate in the midterm elections, so whoever wins this contest would be majority leader in the next Congress. On Tuesday 17 November, Chuck Schumer said he has the votes to be elected majority leader and called the race effectively over. He posted that “I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader”, and urged colleagues to focus on lowering costs and ending corruption.

His challenger is Chris Van Hollen, a Democratic senator from Maryland, who says the country’s election called for change but acknowledges he is the underdog. Van Hollen has criticised Schumer for limiting votes on legislation popular with Democrats, including a bill to boost unions, and backs abolishing the filibuster, a Senate rule that lets opponents hold up votes on most bills. The two also differ on Israel: Schumer has continued to support US aid to Israel, while Van Hollen opposes what he calls “an American taxpayer blank check” to its government.

Counting support is hard. Van Hollen says he has 15 votes. A Punchbowl News tracker reported 14 senators publicly backing Schumer and five backing Van Hollen, with 36 uncommitted, as of Sunday. Schumer’s allies predict he will win more than 40 votes, a claim from his allies rather than his office.

The vote is set for 1 December and will be a closed-door secret ballot, so senators can vote differently from what they say in public; public endorsements therefore offer only a partial picture. Even the winning number is reported differently: both camps speak of a path to 28 votes, while MS NOW says the victor will need at least 29.

The date itself is disputed. Van Hollen, 67, has accused Schumer, 75, who has led Senate Democrats since 2016, of trying to move the vote earlier: “If they really believed that they were ahead, they wouldn’t be trying to move up the elections.” The Boston Globe reports it is not clear the idea has gained traction or is being driven by Schumer himself. Van Hollen has also warned against a “coronation”.

Winning requires a simple majority of the caucus, and Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats next year. Outside the Senate, a Data for Progress poll found that 56% of Democratic-leaning voters said Senate Democrats should choose a new leader, and a plurality favoured Van Hollen. Those voters, however, have no vote in the contest.

economics.headline: US and Thailand Sign a Trade Statement in Manila; Thailand Is to Drop Tariffs While the US Keeps 19%
economics.deck: Trump says Thailand will remove all tariffs on US exports and buy $2.6 billion more in farm goods; the final agreement still needs approval.
body: A tariff is a tax charged on goods imported from abroad. On Tuesday 17 November, on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila, President Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint trade statement. Trump said “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports”.

Trump said Thailand would also remove non-tariff barriers, rules other than taxes that keep goods out, on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry, and would buy an estimated $2.6 billion in additional US agricultural products. A US 19% tariff on Thai goods will remain in place. In 2025, the US had lowered a threatened 36% tariff on Thailand to that 19% level.

The document is not yet a final deal. The White House statement says the two countries “have reached substantial conclusion” in negotiations on an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, and will now begin internal processes to prepare it for signature and entry into force. Bloomberg reported that the text still needs legal and domestic approval. Trump said it would be finalised “in the coming weeks”; Anutin said he was confident it would be ready to sign “real soon”, while acknowledging there is still a little more to do before a binding text. Neither leader announced an implementation date, or what concessions Washington would offer Bangkok in return.

The statement builds on a framework first unveiled in October 2025 at the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur, which covered about 99% of US goods. US trade policy has also shifted since then: Insider Paper reports that the US Supreme Court struck down country-specific tariffs in February, but Washington has since cited insufficient action against forced labour to impose new tariffs on 60 economies, including Thailand. If the terms Trump described hold, American goods would enter Thailand tariff-free, while Thai goods entering the United States would still face the 19% rate.

science_and_technology.headline: Voyager 1, Launched in 1977, Becomes the First Spacecraft to Reach One Light-Day From Earth
science_and_technology.deck: A radio signal now takes 24 hours each way; the probe still runs two of its original ten instruments.
body: NASA’s Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026 at 10:16 UTC, becoming the first spacecraft to do so. A light-day is a unit of distance, not time: the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 25.89 billion kilometres. At the milestone, Voyager 1 is 25.902 billion kilometres, or 16.094 billion miles, from Earth: about 173 astronomical units, where one unit is the average distance between Earth and the Sun. NASA Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker called it “not a time so much as a distance” and an “incredible milestone to celebrate”.

The distance has a practical meaning for the mission team. A command sent from Earth now takes a full 24 hours to reach the probe, and its reply takes another 24 hours to come back, so every exchange is slow. Voyager 1 is tracked by NASA’s Deep Space Network of large antennas in Canberra, California and Madrid, and has travelled at about 38,000 mph, or 17 kilometres per second relative to the Sun, since 1977. The link is fragile: last month NASA lost contact for about 48 hours, and the spacecraft came back online before engineers could send commands to troubleshoot.

Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to fly past Jupiter and Saturn, and crossed into interstellar space, the space between the stars, in August 2012. Its power comes from radioisotope thermoelectric generators, a kind of nuclear battery whose output falls by about 4 watts a year, and the spacecraft grows colder as the power drops. Engineers have therefore switched off heaters and instruments, and its thrusters are clogging. Of the 10 science instruments it launched with, it runs only two, the magnetometer and the plasma wave subsystem, which measure the Sun’s magnetic field and plasma. The team thinks it has enough power to continue to about the early 2030s.

The mission will not last for ever. Spilker has described what the day the signal stops will be like for the people listening on the ground: “We’ll be waiting to hear from Voyager,” she said, “and there won’t be anything.” For Bruce Betts, chief scientist of the Planetary Society, this week’s milestone is above all a testament to the engineers and others who worked on the project.

Its twin, Voyager 2, still runs three science instruments but can now talk only to the Canberra station, and is not expected to reach a light-day from Earth until 2035. Both probes still record data on eight-track tape players, and late next year both will mark 50 years in space. NASA celebrated this week’s milestone by inviting the public to “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day”, flashing lights in Morse code after sunset on 17 November.

explainer.title: How India grades and names cyclones
body: The India Meteorological Department classifies storms over the North Indian Ocean by their sustained wind speed. A low-pressure system becomes a depression at 31-49 km/h and a deep depression at 50-61 km/h. At 62 km/h it becomes a cyclonic storm and is given a name.

Above that, the scale continues: a severe cyclonic storm has winds of 89-117 km/h, a very severe cyclonic storm 118-166 km/h, an extremely severe cyclonic storm 167-221 km/h, and a super cyclonic storm 222 km/h or more. Cyclone Akvan’s forecast landfall winds of 120-130 km/h fall in the very severe band.

Names come from a list drawn up by the 13 member countries of the WMO-ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones, which include India, Bangladesh, Iran, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Each country contributed 13 names, and they are used in turn. Names are used only once, so a storm’s name is never given to a later cyclone.

lead.headline: Four Leaders Meet in Manila
body: On 17 November, leaders of four countries met in Manila. They were from the United States, India, Japan and Australia. Their group is called the Quad.
They talked about critical minerals. These are materials such as lithium, cobalt and nickel. Batteries need them. Trump announced deals so that no single supplier could pressure them.
Their patrol planes will fly together in an exercise in 2027. They will also spend more than $85 million to help the region use trusted AI.

world.headline: Ukraine Damages a Big Bridge to Crimea
body: The Kerch Bridge joins Russia to Crimea. Russia took Crimea from Ukraine in 2014. Putin opened the bridge in 2018.
On 17 November, Ukrainian drones and missiles brought down part of it. Ukraine said one steel arch and the road under it were destroyed.
Russia said the damage was minor. It said trains were running again on one track. The attack came two days before Putin meets Trump and Xi Jinping in China.

india.headline: A Strong Cyclone Heads for Andhra Pradesh
body: Cyclone Akvan is a big storm over the Bay of Bengal. It is getting stronger.
India’s weather office expects it to reach the coast of Andhra Pradesh around noon on 20 November. Winds may reach 120 to 130 km an hour, with gusts up to 145.
Odisha has started moving people to safety. Fishermen must stay off the sea until 20 November. The name Akvan came from Iran.

politics_and_civics.headline: Who Will Lead Senate Democrats?
body: Democrats in the US Senate pick their own leader. Chuck Schumer wants to keep the job. Chris Van Hollen wants to replace him.
Schumer says he has enough votes to win. Van Hollen says he has 15 votes.
The senators will vote on 1 December. The vote is secret. So nobody can be sure who will win until the votes are counted.

economics.headline: The US and Thailand Agree on Trade Steps
body: A tariff is a tax on goods from another country. On 17 November, Trump and Thailand’s leader signed a trade statement in Manila.
Trump said Thailand will drop all tariffs on American goods. It will also buy about $2.6 billion more in American farm goods.
The US will keep its 19% tariff on Thai goods. The deal is not final yet. Trump says it will be finished in the coming weeks.

science_and_technology.headline: Voyager 1 Is Now a Whole Light-Day Away
body: Voyager 1 is a NASA spacecraft. It was launched in 1977.
On 18 November it became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth. That is the distance light travels in 24 hours.
Now a message from Earth takes 24 hours to reach it. Its reply takes another 24 hours. Only two of its 10 instruments still work, and its power is slowly fading.
